title: I Took the Community Olive-Mill Booking to the Chair Who Left My Paste

parts.text: I arrived at the mill at 8:09 a.m. and chair Delfina was already malaxing my numbered paste. The slate said: ONE MILL. TWO HOURS. PASTE STAYS WITH THE BOOKING. I was forty-seven, grove volunteer, holding a lot ticket that listed our fruit. Delfina shrugged. "Chairs are the mill." I photographed the slate, the booking, and her rake in my paste. Then I asked for the mill log. At 8:17 the house pinged why Delfina's name was on my lot. I kept my voice mill-quiet and let the timestamp talk. A slate is only a slate until someone treats it like a clock.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The house can see Delfina's rake in my paste during our booking.

social.video_title: She malaxed my numbered paste on my mill — Part 1/2
social.description: Olive mill, a chair in my paste, a two-hour slate she posted. I logged the rake. Would you have asked for the mill log?

parts.text: Delfina called it a blend until the house asked for the photo. I printed the ticket, the slate, and the rake still. The paste went back to my malaxer. Delfina ran her own two hours and told the next chair atmosphere was always about yield. Yield is a word chairs use when a booking exists. Mill policy now has a second line: CHAIRS ARE NOT THE MILL. I keep our lot on a labeled bin. Delfina brown-bags her jokes. The house finally looks like a booking, not a loan. The rule looks ordinary now, which is the whole point.

social.description: Mill log, numbered paste, and a second line on the slate. Was a blend ever my rake?
